title: Part V: Advanced Prepayment & Greeks
text:
Having constructed forward curves, we return to prepayment. At a high level, borrower prepayments are influenced by two primary drivers:

Refinance Incentive (Refi): Borrowers refinance when market rates drop, allowing a new loan at a lower rate. This is highly sensitive to rate changes.
Demographics (Demo): Life events — job relocation, retirement, family changes, downsizing — also drive prepayments. These are less rate-sensitive and more tied to the borrower’s circumstances and the loan’s age.



The mortgage rate from the market is known as the Primary Current Coupon (PCC). To project it into the future, we use a simple model:
\[
PCC(t) = \text{DiscountRate}(t) + \text{PccSpread}
\]
where \(\text{DiscountRate}(t)\) is the short rate and PccSpread is a fixed spread accounting for additional costs. Use 3.3% as your spread.



The refinance component is:
\[
\text{refi}(\text{spread}(t)) =
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } \text{spread} < 0 \\
\text{slope} \cdot \text{spread} & \text{if } 0 \leq \text{spread} \leq 0.015 \\
0.0425 & \text{if } \text{spread} > 0.015
\end{cases}
\]
where:

\(\text{slope} = \dfrac{0.0425}{0.015}\)
\(\text{spread}(t) = \text{GrossCoupon} - PCC(t)\)




Demographic prepayments depend on loan age and seasonal trends:
\[\text{demo}(t) = \text{seasoning}(\text{age}(t)) \cdot \text{seasonal}(\text{month\_of\_year}(t))\]

Seasoning: Prepayments ramp linearly from 0 to a base SMM over the first 18 months. Use 0.5% as your base SMM.
Seasonality: Rates exhibit seasonal trends with summer peaks and winter dips. Use the monthly scalars below.

SEASONAL_FACTORS_ARRAY = np.array([
    0.75,  # January
    0.84,  # February
    0.93,  # March
    1.02,  # April
    1.11,  # May
    1.20,  # June
    1.20,  # July
    1.11,  # August
    1.02,  # September
    0.93,  # October
    0.84,  # November
    0.75   # December
])



\[SMM(t) = \text{refi}(\text{spread}(t)) + \text{demo}(t)\]
where \(t\) is time in months from the first of the market close’s month (e.g., if market close is 1/15/2024, then \(t\) is measured from 1/1/2024).
Implement the above. Run our 15-year MBS using the rates from Problem 10 with OAS of 3%. Then run the same MBS with discount rates shocked +0.5% and −0.5%. Plot the balances through time for each scenario.

NB: Changing OAS should not change cash flows. Shocking discount rates will change cash flows because PCC is a function of those rates. Make sure you verify this distinction.

title: Part V: Advanced Prepayment & Greeks
text:
Problem 19: Derivatives
The Taylor series gives us a second-order approximation to the change in MBS value given a change in rates.
The first derivative with respect to rates is the Dollar Value of an 01 (DV01). These exercises use 1% as the shift amount.
\[DV01 = \frac{V(\text{up}) - V(\text{dn})}{2 \cdot \text{shock}}\]
The second derivative is convexity (or gamma):
\[\text{Convexity} = \frac{V(\text{up}) + V(\text{dn}) - 2 \cdot V(\text{mid})}{\text{shock}^2}\]
where \(V(\text{mid})\) is the base value (shock = 0).

title: Part VI: Monte Carlo
text:
To generate Monte Carlo paths of rates we use the classic Hull-White model for short rates.



The one-factor Hull-White model describes the evolution of short-term interest rates \(r(t)\) via the stochastic differential equation (SDE):
\[dr(t) = [\theta(t) - \alpha r(t)]\, dt + \sigma\, dW(t)\]
Key components:

Mean Reversion: The term \(-\alpha r(t)\) pulls \(r(t)\) toward a time-dependent mean. \(\alpha > 0\) is the mean reversion speed.
Volatility: \(\sigma\) is the volatility of the short rate, scaled by Brownian motion \(W(t)\).
Time-Dependent Drift \(\theta(t)\): Ensures the model fits the initial term structure of interest rates.




Using the Euler-Maruyama scheme:
\[r_{t+\Delta t} = r_t + (\theta(t) - \alpha r_t)\,\Delta t + \sigma \sqrt{\Delta t}\, Z_t\]
where:

\(r_t\): Short rate from your forward curve at time \(t\)
\(\Delta t\): Time step size
\(Z_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\): Standard normal draw

To compute \(\theta(t_i)\):
\[\theta(t_i) = \frac{f_{t_{i+1}} - f_{t_i}}{\Delta t} + \alpha f_{t_i} + \frac{\sigma^2}{2\alpha}\left(1 - e^{-2\alpha t_i}\right)\]
where \(f_t\) is the continuously compounded forward rate from your forward curve. Choose your grid so that \(t\) always hits a knot point on your step discount rate function — no interpolation required.



Each Monte Carlo path produces a rate function that can be used to discount future cash flows. Our discount factors are now stochastic (SDF). The SDFs are not zero coupon bonds. However, the average of pathwise SDFs equals the corresponding ZCB:
\[ZCB(t, T) = \mathbb{E}[\text{SDF}(t, T)] = \mathbb{E}\!\left[e^{-\int_t^T r(u)\,du}\right]\]




Initialize: Set the starting short rate \(r_0\) from the initial rate of your forward curve.
Iterate: For each time step, compute \(r_{t+\Delta t}\) using the discretized equation.
Simulate paths: Repeat across multiple paths by drawing independent \(Z_t\) for each.
Aggregate: Use the simulated paths to compute expectations, price derivatives, or analyze rate distributions.


NB: Smaller \(\Delta t\) improves accuracy but increases computational cost. Variance reduction techniques are explored in Problem 23.




Example Output:
Results for a 28-day (\(28/365\) year) time step grid with \(\sigma = 0.01\) and \(\alpha = 0.03\):
The variance of the simulated short rate \(r_t\) should be approximately: \[\frac{\sigma^2}{2\alpha}\left(1 - e^{-2\alpha t}\right)\]
The variance of SDF(\(t\)) should be approximately: \[\left(\frac{\sigma}{\alpha}\right)^2 \left(t + \frac{2}{\alpha}e^{-\alpha t} - \frac{1}{2\alpha}e^{-2\alpha t} - \frac{3}{2\alpha}\right)\]

title: Part II: Prepayment & Dates
text:
Recall that we allow the borrower to prepay their loan. There are a number of reasons why this may happen:

The borrower gets a job in a new city
The borrower finds a lower rate in the current market
The borrower outgrows (or downsizes from) their current home
The borrower takes out a new loan with a higher balance and pockets the difference (Cash Out)

We referred to projected balances as “scheduled” in previous exercises because they don’t include prepayments. The Single Monthly Mortality (SMM) rate is the percentage of the pool that prepays in a particular month. We use it to compute the fraction of the original pool that remains:
\[pool(0) = 1\]
\[pool(t) = pool(t-1) \cdot [1 - SMM(t-1)]\]
We use this to project the actual balance (\(B\)):
\[B(t) = \text{ScheduledBalance}(t) \cdot pool(t)\]
Create a function that takes the term in months, gross coupon, net coupon, initial balance, and a vector of SMMs, and returns a time series including month, balance, net interest paid, and principal paid for a pass-through bond with prepayment.

NB: One cannot technically prepay in the period from \(M-1\) to \(M\) because all pools pay off at maturity under our assumptions.

title: Part II: Prepayment & Dates
text:
Problem 8: Weighted Average Life
The common perception of a bond is one of a bullet, where the balance remains constant until maturity. A mortgage bond, however, amortizes throughout its life — the balance changes before maturity. For an amortizing bond, the Weighted Average Life (WAL) gives a sense of the average time it takes for the investor to receive all their principal back.
Further reading: Weighted-average life (Wikipedia)
Write a function that takes a vector of balances, a vector of accrual dates, a vector of payment dates, and a reference date, and computes the WAL.

A note on the reference date
The reference date is the trade settle date — the day the investor pays for and takes ownership of the bond. There is a subtlety about which future cash flows the investor owns. The investor is entitled to all cash flows based on the balance of the bond at time of purchase. For example, if one buys a bond on the 5th of the month and the payment delay is 24 days, the next cash flow falls on the 25th. The investor is not entitled to this cash flow because it is based on the previous month’s balance.
Assume 365 days in a year when computing the number of years between payment dates and the settle date.

This set of exercises grew from a capstone project led with students from Emory University’s MSBA program. The original problems were designed to familiarize students with basic mortgage concepts under idealized conditions. The content has since expanded to cover fixed-rate bonds, forward curve calibration, prepayment modeling, and Monte Carlo pricing. This is a work in progress — future additions will include trinomial lattices, PCAs, and C++.

title: Introduction to Mortgage Analytics
text:
How to Use These Exercises
Work through the problems in order. Each one builds on the last. Implement your solutions in Python, applying the industry practices described below.

title: Introduction to Mortgage Analytics
text:
Industry Standards
While solving these problems, use standard tools and techniques from the software industry:

DevOps
Coding standards
Git
Code reviews
Automated testing (unit, regression, etc.)
Debuggers and profilers
VS Code, Lint, CoPilot

This is an opportunity to move from student to production coding.

title: Introduction to Mortgage Analytics
text:
Clean Code Principles
There are many excellent books on writing clean code. Here are key principles to guide you:

Put most logic in Python modules. Create a single top-level demo.py to demonstrate functionality.
Use well-named variables. They make code easier to read and reduce documentation burden.
Validate inputs — check that a divisor isn’t zero, that a price is non-negative, etc.
Avoid global variables, except for constants.
Strive for clarity and maintainability over raw speed. Write as if handing the code to someone else.
Avoid premature optimization. Let your profiler guide you.
Document your API. Does it feel like a natural interface to another programmer?
Do not use magic numbers or strings. Put them in named variables.
Do not copy and paste code. Refactor shared logic into functions. Keep your code DRY (Don’t Repeat Yourself).
Separate IO from logic. Business logic should not depend on a particular data source.
Use unit tests. They are your safety net when refactoring.
Keep functions short — ideally no longer than a page.
Avoid computing the same thing twice. Move invariants outside loops.
Leverage vectorization via NumPy. Python loops are slow.
Think like a mathematician. Calculus can make your code cleaner and faster.
Track units. Are values decimal or percent? Confusion here causes hard-to-find bugs.
Use docstrings. NumPy format is recommended.

title: Introduction to Mortgage Analytics
text:
A Note on LLMs
Do not overuse LLMs. The point of these exercises is to learn. Having an LLM solve the problems for you defeats the purpose. They are excellent as an advanced manual or documentation rough-draft generator — but the main logic should be yours.

title: Introduction to Mortgage Analytics
text:
Assumptions
Please review these periodically:

All mortgages are fixed-rate loans with no interest-only periods.
Payments are made on the first of each month, with no partial accruals or defaults.
The amount paid is either the scheduled payment or the full remaining balance plus interest. Curtailments are not modeled.
A pool consists of loans that are identical in balance, coupon, origination, and term.
No accrual period will start on a day of month greater than 28. This avoids month-end complications.
No special treatment for holidays or weekends.
If a settle date lands exactly at the end of an accrual period, the investor is not entitled to that period’s cash flow.

title: Part I: Mortgage Basics
text:
The length of a loan is known as its term. Common terms include 15 and 30 years. We sometimes refer to an original term to differentiate it from the remaining term, which is the remaining life of an aged loan. For clarity:
\[
\text{term} = \text{original term} = \text{age} + \text{remaining term}
\]
A borrower must pay an interest rate for a mortgage, known as its coupon. For reasons that will be clear later, we will refer to the borrower’s coupon as the gross coupon. This coupon is quoted as an annual rate, but we will always divide it by 12 (the number of months in a year) when computing owed interest. The interest owed is the loan balance at the beginning of the period times the coupon divided by 12.
Given a term \(M\) in months, a gross coupon \(C\), and an initial loan amount \(B\), derive a formula for the constant monthly payment \(P\) such that:
\[B(0) = B\]
\[B(1) = B(0) \cdot (1 + C/12) - P\]
\[\vdots\]
\[B(t) = B(t-1) \cdot (1 + C/12) - P\]
\[\vdots\]
\[B(M) = 0\]

NB: If you haven’t reviewed geometric series recently, you might want to revisit the topic.

title: Part I: Mortgage Basics
text:
Problem 4: Mortgage Backed Securities
When creating a Mortgage Backed Security (MBS), a financial institution combines many “similar” loans into a single pool and sells them to an investor. In many cases, the institution creates a Pass-Through bond: they continue to collect the borrower’s payments, take a small Servicing Fee (typically 0.25% of the pool balance), and pass the remaining amount to the investor. The investor is entitled to all the principal paid, but the servicing fee comes out of the interest. The Net Coupon is the gross coupon less the servicing fee (we assume all other fees are zero).

NB: Scheduled balances are computed with the gross coupon, but the interest paid to the investor is computed with the net coupon.

It is convenient to think of a pool of loans as a single loan, where attributes such as the gross coupon are the balance-weighted average of the individual loans in the pool, and the balance is the sum of the individual balances.
Assume the loan from the previous exercises is actually a pool. Add a new column representing the net interest paid to the investor, where the servicing fee is 0.25%.

title: Part III: Discounting & Pricing
text:
Consider a bank account that accrues interest continuously at rate \(r\). If we invest \(B(0)\) dollars today, after two years we have:
\[B(2) = B(0) \cdot e^{2r}\]
which implies:
\[B(0) = \frac{1}{e^{2r}} = e^{-2r}\]
\(B(0)\) is today’s value of a dollar paid two years in the future. It is also the price of a Zero Coupon Bond (ZCB) — a bond that pays one dollar at maturity but accrues no interest during its life.
ZCBs are closely related to Discount Factors (DFs). In general, if we have a function \(r(t)\) that produces continuously compounded discount rates, the discount factor for the period from \(t\) to \(T\) is:
\[DF(t, T) = e^{-\int_t^T r(u)\, du}\]
In the special case where \(r(u)\) comes from a forward curve, the ZCB and DF are equivalent. We will revisit this distinction in future exercises.

NB: \(ZCB(t, T) = \dfrac{ZCB(0, T)}{ZCB(0, t)}\)

Implement a function that computes ZCBs at arbitrary dates greater than or equal to market close. You will pass it \(r(t)\), which for now we assume is a step function. We also assume 365 days in a year. Use the rates provided in the code block below and assume the knots are the first of every month starting at 10/1/2024.

        0.034238589, 0.033344373, 0.032562165, 0.031897518, 0.031350018, 0.030912406,

Problem 10: Present Value
Now that we can compute ZCBs, we can compute the time-\(t\) value \(V(t)\) by taking the dot product of the vector of future cash flows with a vector of ZCBs corresponding to the payment dates (not accrual dates) relative to time \(t\).
The basic steps are:

Use the settle and accrual dates to determine which cash flows the investor purchased
Use the settle date to determine \(t\) for discounting
For each relevant payment date \(T_n\), compute \(ZCB(t, T_n)\)
Take the dot product of your cash flow and ZCB vectors to compute \(V(t)\)

When \(t > 0\), the quantity computed is called a forward value — the number of dollars at which one would buy or sell the instrument at time \(t\).

Problem 11: Price
In Problem 10 we computed the present value of all future cash flows relative to the trade settle date. Now we want to compute how the bond price would be quoted in the market, ultimately arriving at the clean price.
First, normalize the value by multiplying by 100 and dividing by the balance at the settle date. This gives the dirty price:
\[\text{Dirty Price} = \text{Value} \times \frac{100}{\text{Balance at Settle}}\]
For background on clean and dirty prices, and accrued interest, see:

Dirty Price (Wikipedia)
Clean Price (Wikipedia)
Day Count Convention (Wikipedia)

Our bond uses the 30/360 day count method. Compute the interest accrued from the partial period running from the first of the trade settle month to the trade settle date. Excel’s DAYS360 function is a useful reference.

Problem 12: Option Adjusted Spread
The prices generated using the above logic often differ from market-observed MBS prices. To reconcile this, an Option Adjusted Spread (OAS) is added to the discount rates.
For simplicity, work with values rather than prices. Given a discount date grid, discount rate grid, settlement date, cash flows, and a target value, write a function to compute the OAS that aligns the computed price with the target value.

NB: This involves discounting only. It does not change cash flows. The OAS is a constant spread applied to the continuously compounded discount rates. Since spreads may vary across securities, do not adjust the discount rates directly.


NB: A technical simplification is made for forward settles. The forward value equation used here is: \[V(t, OAS) = \frac{V(0, OAS)}{ZCB(t, OAS)}\] rather than the technically correct: \[V(t, OAS) = \frac{V(0, OAS)}{ZCB(t, 0)}\]

To calibrate a forward curve using market inputs, we first need to generate cash flows for our calibration instruments. Each cash flow includes the coupon payment (balance * coupon / 2), with the final cash flow also including principal repayment. Raise an error if the day of month is greater than 28.

title: Part IV: Forward Curves
text:
Problem 14: Forward Curve — Bootstrapping
A forward curve of instantaneous discount rates maps future points in time to discount rates. This function helps determine the present value of cash flows occurring at those specific future dates. The formulas are the same as in Problem 9.
Forward curves aren’t directly observable — they must be calibrated from market prices or yields. A common misunderstanding is that forward rates represent the market’s forecast of future rates. In fact, forward rates tell you the rates you can lock in today for accrual periods starting in the future. They reflect what you can secure today for a future period, not necessarily what the market expects rates to be.
The simplest calibration technique is the bootstrap method, which constructs a curve from observed prices of calibration securities. Our calibration instruments are CMTs. To begin:

Select a market close date from the Treasury Department’s CMT website and gather par yields for maturities from 1 to 30 years.
Create a date grid starting from the close date that includes each bond’s maturity date.
Construct a step function of instantaneous, continuously compounded discount rates with knots based on the maturity grid.
The method is called a “bootstrap” because you solve sequentially: find the constant rate from 0 to 1 year that produces par for the 1-year bond, lock it in, then solve for the 2-year, and so on until the 30-year bond.


NB: Your ZCB calculator may have assumed a uniform grid of discount rates. You may need to generalize it to handle an arbitrary step function structure.

Problem 15: Forward Bond Rates
Now that you have a forward curve, write a function to calculate the coupon rate required to produce a par price for a given semi-annual bond. The function should take a start date \(t\) (\(\geq\) market close) and a maturity date \(T\) (\(\geq t\)). If \(t\) is the market close and \(T\) matches one of your calibration maturities, the function should reproduce the exact coupon from calibration. When \(t >\) market close, the function produces a “forward” bond rate — the rate you can lock in today for a bond starting at time \(t\).

title: Part IV: Forward Curves
section: Problem 16: Forward Curve — An Improved Calibration Method
text:
Problem 16: Forward Curve — An Improved Calibration Method
The discount rate grid from our bootstrapper is very coarse, which can produce large jumps in rates. Develop an alternative calibrator that uses a step function with a finer grid (monthly or weekly intervals) to produce the same spot bond prices while penalizing large rate jumps. This new calibrator should minimize rate jumps via a penalty function, ensuring smoother transitions. You have a lot of freedom here — be creative.
Apply this new curve with the coupon rate function from Problem 15. The output for spot calibration instruments should remain unchanged, but forward rates may differ significantly. Plot both the original and new forward curves to visualize the differences.
In practice, the “knots” at the front end of the curve are often based on Federal Reserve meeting dates, where rate changes are expected. The back end typically follows a more regular structure with larger intervals.

NB: This will take considerably longer to run than your bootstrap.
